title: Theatre of Dionysus
notes: p1.1: the stone theatre and columned stage building are the later stone theatre (4th century BC and after); in Euripides' day the seats and stage building were simpler. Narration does not describe the building, so no patch needed.
p1.3: art shows a modern girl with a pink-bowed owl in the ancient crowd (the player and Glauka). Narration uses it ('That's you and me').
p2.2: the 'Euripides' Hecuba, 424 BC' tag is lettered on this panel and the caption on p2.3 repeats it. Narrated over; optional patch to remove the tag.
p2.4: shows an empty theatre that is not obviously this one. Harmless.

p3.1/p3.2: the surviving marble throne dates from well after Euripides (Hellenistic/Roman); the priest in 424 BC sat on an earlier seat. The card says 'He had the best view', which stays true; narration does not date the throne. p3.1 carving (winged lions, shield) is invented; the real throne has different reliefs. Low priority.
p2.3: climax panel is deliberately short and ends on 'Then the queen weeps.'

panels.visual: Wide view of the Theatre of Dionysus on the slope of the Acropolis, rows of ancient Athenians on the hillside, a stage below, sunlit
panels.caption: Theatre was born on this slope.
panels.narr: Theatre was born on this slope, right where you're sitting. I saw the very first plays. Well, from a tree near the top.

panels.visual: Three ancient playwrights (Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides) shown side by side as portrait busts with name plaques, each holding a scroll
panels.caption: Plays by Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides had their first performances here.
panels.narr: Three names to know: Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides. Their plays had their first performances here, on this hillside. Here they are as marble busts. Back then they were writers with a new play.

panels.visual: Thousands of spectators sitting in rows up the hillside, cushions and sunhats, a huge crowd
panels.caption: Up to about sixteen thousand people watched.
panels.narr: Up to about sixteen thousand people watched, once the stone seats were built. They packed the rows with cushions and sunhats. Find the girl with the owl beside her. That's you and me.

panels.visual: The orchestra circle with a chorus of masked men in robes, dancing in a ring, dust rising
panels.caption: Everyone watched from the hillside.
panels.narr: Everyone watched from the hillside while the chorus danced in a ring below, stamping up the dust. Look at their faces: masks, every one. Backstage, one man was getting ready.

panels.visual: Backstage view of three actors holding large masks with painted faces, putting them on
panels.caption: All the actors were men in masks.
panels.narr: All the actors were men in masks. Backstage they pulled on painted faces: a grin, a scowl, a scream. Put one on and you were a king, a slave or a god.

panels.visual: An actor in a queen's mask (woman's face, tragic expression) and a long robe, but with the broad shoulders of a man
panels.caption: Even when they played queens.
panels.narr: Even when they played queens. This one is Hecuba, queen of Troy. Look closely: a woman's face, a long robe and a man's big arms. The audience saw only the queen.

panels.visual: Close-up of the Queen Hecuba mask with a tear painted on it, dramatic stage lighting
panels.caption: Euripides' Hecuba was performed here around 424 BC.
panels.narr: Euripides' Hecuba was performed here around 424 BC. Troy has fallen. Her children are taken from her, one by one. Then the queen weeps.

panels.visual: The empty stage with a clear sign of no women: a crossed-out ladies silhouette in a thought bubble over a puzzled Glauka
panels.caption: No women stood on this stage.
panels.narr: No women stood on this stage. Every queen, every mother, every goddess was a man in a mask. The saddest woman in Troy was played by a man.

panels.visual: The front row of the theatre with marble thrones; the marble throne of the priest of Dionysus in the middle, richly carved
panels.caption: In the front row, in the middle, is the marble throne of the priest of Dionysus.
panels.narr: Now look at the front row, in the middle. That's the marble throne of the priest of Dionysus, the god this whole theatre was built for.

panels.visual: The priest of Dionysus in a rich robe and a wreath sitting comfortably on his throne with a cushion and a drink
panels.caption: He had the best view in the theatre.
panels.narr: He had the best view in the theatre, close enough to see every mask. Look at him: a soft cushion and a cup in his hand.

panels.visual: Modern view of the same throne in ruins on a sunny day with little tourists posing next to it
panels.caption: It is still there.
panels.narr: It is still there, cracked and worn, in the same front row. Tourists stop to photograph it every day. Now you know who sat in it.

panels.visual: Glauka the owl sitting on the arm of the marble throne and facing us proudly
panels.caption: Take your seat.

speech.speaker: Glauka
speech.text: The best view in the house.

panels.narr: That's history: it happened, and here's how we know. Euripides' Hecuba still survives, and the priest's seat is still in the front row. Climb higher, look down at the stage, and picture the queen.
